doc.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Outside Basie: Monk, Coltrane, Elvin Jones
title: Playing with Kenny Clarke and the energy of Elvin
summary: Clarke was on his first record, but no one matches Elvin's energy, where Foster picked his own 'one'.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Can I just ask another question? Kenny Clarke, you played with Kenny Clarke. You played with Boo, Art Blakey. You played with Elvin. But what was playing with Kenny Clarke like?

It was great. I loved it. I played with Kenny Clarke with one of my -- he was on my first recording session, Here’s Comes Frank Foster, done in 1954. I played with him on a couple of other subsequent recordings. I’m ashamed not to remember, but it was a good experience. But no experience will stand out like that of playing with Elvin. That was --

The sheer energy, along with the challenge of trying to measure up to that energy level, as well as maintain the type of musicality that I would like to be associated with, and just taking in all that excitement. It was just exciting, highly

exciting playing with Elvin. He didn’t like real fast tempos, but he didn’t have to. We didn’t have to play breakneck tempos. We could play medium tempos. Playing with Elvin was just -- you got that feeling, whatever the tempo was. I know you have heard of “knowing where the one is.” Like, okay, a measure of music was one, two, three, four. The one is very important, because it’s the first beat in a measure. If you don’t know where one is, you’re likely to be very lost. When you speak of drummers who don’t know where one is, you’re saying that their rhythmic concept is out to lunch. With Elvin sometimes, we’d go so far out there that I couldn’t hear where one was. I would lose the one, but everything would be so exciting that I could just say, I’m going to pick a spot where I want one to be. I would say -- way out there, I would say, right here, boom, that’s going to be my one, and it would end up that I was always right
You mean one as a point of resolution?
One as a point of, yeah, of a beginning, of a beginning point.
When you’re going to come out from being out there, you can only come back by finding one.
That’s one way of looking at it.
That’s why I made my point of resolution.
